title: Mock 4 · Applied Basics
blurb: Everyday rules and first strategy questions across MF, SIF and both derivative modules.

questions.q: A long-term asset mix set according to an investor's goals and risk profile, rebalanced periodically, is known as:
questions.explanation: Strategic = long-term policy mix; tactical = temporary deviation to exploit market opportunities.
hints: Wrong — tactical allocation is a short-term tilt based on market views.
Wrong — market timing is trying to predict entry/exit points.
Correct — strategic allocation is the long-term, goal-linked mix.
Wrong — sector rotation shifts between sectors, not the overall asset mix.

questions.q: How many investment strategies can an AMC launch under each SIF category (e.g., Equity Long-Short)?
options: No limit, subject to SEBI approval
questions.explanation: In line with MF scheme categorisation, only one investment strategy is permitted under each SIF category.
hints: Wrong — the cap is one.
Wrong — the cap is one.
Wrong — a one-per-category cap applies, as with MF categorisation.
Correct — to avoid proliferation, only one strategy per category is permitted.

questions.q: If an SIF investment strategy is launched as a close-ended or interval structure, its units must be:
options: Listed on a recognised stock exchange
questions.explanation: The workbook notes the listing requirement for close-ended and interval structures applies to SIFs as well.
hints: Wrong — MF/SIF units are held in demat or SoA form; listing is required here.
Correct — the listing provision for close-ended/interval schemes applies to SIF too.
Wrong — interval/close-ended structures do not offer daily redemption.
Wrong — no such restriction is stated.

questions.q: Within how many days must an AMC redress an investor grievance?
questions.explanation: AMCs shall redress grievances promptly and not later than 21 calendar days; investors may escalate to SCORES and SMART ODR.
hints: Correct — the 2026 regulations require redressal within 21 calendar days.
Wrong — 30 days is not the current limit.
Wrong — 7 working days is not the rule.
Wrong — 45 days is not the rule.

questions.q: Within what time must an AMC disclose the risk band of all its SIF investment strategies on its website?
options: Within 30 days from the close of each quarter
Within 10 days from the close of each month
Only once a year as on 31 March
questions.explanation: SIF Risk-Band: assigned at NFO, evaluated monthly, disclosed within 10 days of month close; annual 31 March disclosure with number of changes on AMC and AMFI sites.
hints: Wrong — quarterly disclosure is not the rule.
Correct — Risk-Band is evaluated monthly and disclosed within 10 days of month-end.
Wrong — fortnightly within 5 days applies to debt MF portfolio disclosure.
Wrong — the 31 March disclosure is in addition to monthly disclosure.

questions.q: If an investor changes the distributor code in a folio, trail commission is:
options: Paid to the new distributor immediately
Paid to the old distributor for 12 months
Not paid to any distributor for 12 months
questions.explanation: On change of distributor, no trail commission is payable to any distributor for a period of 12 months.
hints: Wrong — the new distributor waits 12 months.
Wrong — the old distributor also stops receiving trail.
Wrong — there is no split.
Correct — to prevent malpractice, no trail is paid to either for 12 months.

questions.q: The maximum total expense ratio for an index fund or ETF is:
questions.explanation: Index fund/ETF TER (including investment & advisory fees) ≤ 0.90% of daily net assets.
hints: Wrong — 1.00% applies to close-ended equity schemes.
Wrong — 2.10% is the first slab for active equity schemes.
Correct — index funds/ETFs are capped at 0.90%.
Wrong — 0.70% is the balance-asset slab for non-equity schemes.

questions.q: Stamp duty on the issue of mutual fund units (purchase, SIP, STP, IDCW reinvestment) is levied at:
questions.explanation: Stamp duty: 0.005% on issue of units; 0.015% on transfer of units (since 1 July 2020).
hints: Correct — issue of units attracts 0.005% stamp duty.
Wrong — 0.015% applies to transfer of units.
Wrong — 0.001% is the STT rate on redemption of equity units.
Wrong — not the prescribed rate.

questions.q: A redemption request for an equity fund is received at 2.15 pm on a business day. Which NAV applies?
options: The NAV of the day the money reaches the investor
questions.explanation: Non-liquid redemptions: cut-off 3 pm; before cut-off — same day NAV; after — next business day NAV.
hints: Wrong — next-day NAV applies after 3 pm.
Wrong — previous-day NAV applies to liquid fund purchases.
Wrong — NAV is fixed by time of receipt, not of payout.
Correct — redemptions received before the 3 pm cut-off get same-day NAV.

questions.q: A switch from one scheme to another is treated as:
options: A non-financial transaction with no tax impact
A redemption from one scheme and a purchase in another, combined in one transaction
A transfer of units between investors
questions.explanation: Switch = redemption + purchase in one transaction; exit load and capital gains tax may apply on the switch-out.
hints: Wrong — the redemption leg can trigger capital gains.
Correct — a switch has a redemption leg (load/tax may apply) and a purchase leg.
Wrong — units do not change hands between investors.
Wrong — it is unrelated to IDCW reinvestment.

questions.q: For a salaried investor aiming to build wealth over 15 years who does not need regular income, which option is generally more suitable?
options: IDCW reinvestment option for tax savings
questions.explanation: Growth option defers tax until redemption and lets returns compound — better for long-term wealth creation.
hints: Correct — growth allows tax deferral and compounding.
Wrong — payouts are taxed at slab and break compounding.
Wrong — IDCW reinvested is still taxed at slab each time.
Wrong — daily IDCW is for very short-term debt needs.

questions.q: A diversified equity scheme earned 14% with a beta of 1.6 when the risk-free rate was 6%. What is its Treynor ratio?
questions.explanation: Treynor ratio = (Rs − Rf) ÷ Beta; it uses beta (market risk), unlike Sharpe which uses standard deviation.
hints: Wrong — 14 ÷ 1.6 ignores the risk-free rate.
Wrong — 6 ÷ 1.6 uses the risk-free rate instead of the premium.
Wrong — that inverts the ratio.

questions.q: Under Section 18A of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, derivative contracts are legal and valid if they are:
options: Signed by both parties before a notary
Traded on a recognised stock exchange and settled on its clearing house as per its rules
questions.explanation: Section 18A: contracts in derivatives are legal and valid if traded on a recognised exchange and settled on its clearing house (or as notified by the Central Government).
hints: Wrong — notarisation is irrelevant.
Wrong — SEBI does not approve each contract.
Correct — Section 18A validates exchange-traded, clearing-house-settled derivatives.
Wrong — RBI registration is not the condition.

questions.q: A price-weighted index has three stocks priced at ₹100, ₹200 and ₹300 on the base date. Today they are ₹150, ₹220 and ₹330. What is today's index level (no divisor adjustment)?
questions.explanation: Price-weighted index = sum of prices ÷ number of stocks.
hints: Wrong — 200 is the base-date level.
Wrong — 700 is the sum of prices, not divided by 3.
Wrong — that is the percentage of the base level.

questions.q: An investor holds a ₹40 lakh equity portfolio with a beta of 1.2. Nifty futures trade at 24,000 with a lot size of 50. How many lots should be sold to hedge fully?
questions.explanation: Hedge contracts = (Portfolio value × beta) ÷ (futures price × lot size).
hints: Wrong — that ignores beta.
Wrong — not supported by the formula.
Wrong — not supported by the formula.

questions.q: If index futures are trading above their fair (theoretical) price, the arbitrage opportunity is:
options: Cash-and-carry arbitrage: buy in the cash market and sell futures
Reverse cash-and-carry: sell in the cash market and buy futures
Calendar spread: buy near month and sell far month
questions.explanation: Futures > fair value ⇒ cash-and-carry; futures < fair value ⇒ reverse cash-and-carry.
hints: Correct — overpriced futures are sold against a cash purchase.
Wrong — reverse cash-and-carry applies when futures are underpriced.
Wrong — calendar spreads exploit mispricing between expiries.
Wrong — mispricing outside no-arbitrage bounds creates opportunity.

questions.q: Theta of an option measures:
options: The change in premium for a change in volatility
The change in the option premium due to the passage of time (time decay)
The change in delta for a change in the underlying
The change in premium for a change in interest rates
questions.explanation: Greeks: delta (price), gamma (delta change), theta (time), vega (volatility), rho (interest rate).
hints: Wrong — that is vega.
Correct — theta captures time decay.
Wrong — that is gamma.
Wrong — that is rho.

questions.q: With all other factors unchanged, a put option with a higher strike price will have:
questions.explanation: Strike ↑ ⇒ call premium ↓ and put premium ↑.
hints: Wrong — lower premium for higher strike applies to calls.
Wrong — strike affects the premium.
Wrong — premium remains positive before expiry.
Correct — a higher strike raises a put's intrinsic value.

questions.q: A long strangle is created by:
options: Buying a call and a put with the same strike and expiry
Selling an OTM call and an OTM put
Buying an OTM call and an OTM put with different strikes and the same expiry
Buying one ITM call, selling two ATM calls and buying one OTM call
questions.explanation: Long strangle: long OTM call + long OTM put; maximum loss = total premium; profits from a big move either way.
hints: Wrong — that is a long straddle.
Wrong — that is a short strangle.
Correct — a long strangle uses two OTM options, making it cheaper than a straddle.
Wrong — that is a long call butterfly.

questions.q: Put open interest in an index option series is 15,000 contracts and call open interest is 10,000 contracts. The put-call ratio is:
questions.explanation: PCR = Put OI (or volume) ÷ Call OI (or volume).
hints: Correct — PCR = put OI ÷ call OI = 15,000 ÷ 10,000.
Wrong — that is call ÷ put.
Wrong — that is the total OI.
Wrong — that is the difference.

questions.q: A yield curve where long-term yields are higher than short-term yields is called:
questions.explanation: Normal yield curve reflects term and inflation-risk premia for longer maturities.
hints: Wrong — inverted curves have short yields above long yields.
Wrong — flat means similar yields across maturities.
Wrong — humped means medium-term yields are highest.
Correct — a normal curve slopes upward with maturity.

questions.q: An interest rate collar is created by:
options: Buying an interest rate cap and selling an interest rate floor
Buying a floor and selling a cap
Buying both a cap and a floor
questions.explanation: Collar = buy cap + sell floor on the same rate, maturity and notional; reverse collar = buy floor + sell cap.
hints: Correct — the floor premium received offsets the cap cost.
Wrong — that is a reverse collar.
Wrong — buying both is not a collar.
Wrong — swaps are not options.

questions.q: A trader buys 4 lots of 91-day T-bill futures at a quoted price of 94.00. What is the contract value?
questions.explanation: T-bill futures contract value = 2,000 × (100 − 0.25y) per lot; here y = 100 − 94 = 6.
hints: Wrong — that uses 94 directly as the price.
Wrong — that ignores the yield.
Wrong — that is the value of a single lot.

questions.q: Exchange-traded interest rate options on GOI securities in India are:
questions.explanation: IRO specs: premium-style European calls/puts, lot FV ₹2 lakh, cash settlement T+1.
hints: Wrong — they are European and cash-settled.
Correct — they are premium-style European calls and puts, cash-settled.
Wrong — not Bermudan.
Wrong — the premium is paid upfront.

questions.q: Which is a key limitation of exchange-traded interest rate derivatives for hedgers?
options: They cannot be traded by banks
Standardised, cash-settled contracts on limited underlyings can leave basis risk
questions.explanation: ETIRDs are standardised and mainly cash-settled; underlyings and tenors are limited, so hedges may be imperfect (basis risk).
hints: Wrong — the clearing corporation removes counterparty risk.
Wrong — banks participate actively.
Wrong — exchange trading is transparent.
Correct — mismatch in instrument, tenor and expiry dates causes imperfect hedges.
